stories.text:
The house was designed in 1781 for the Smith family as Wilford Hall, the centre of an estate with stables, lodges for the house staff and a private chapel.[^walk] It is a red-brick country house of three storeys and five bays, listed Grade II, and its stable block of the same year is listed too. The Smiths' bank in Nottingham is believed to have been the first bank outside London, and Samuel Smith, an MP for 44 years, is believed to have built the house; by 1790 it was his.[^throsby] The banker Abel Smith died at Wilford on 12 July 1788.[^s1][^s2] His wife's younger sister, Elizabeth Bird, was the mother of William Wilberforce, the slavery abolitionist, who stayed at the house for several months between 1786 and 1789.[^s1][^s2][^s3] In 1853 it was the seat of Henry Smith, a large, handsome brick mansion; he owned about 70 acres of the parish, and in 1828 he built an infant school in the village.[^white]

Thomas Forman, who founded the Nottingham Post, later bought the house from the Smiths, and it passed to the Forman Hardy family; at some point it was renamed Wilford House.[^s1] It became offices in the 1980s, the Wilford Place estate was built on its grounds in 2006,[^trail] and in 2021 the house was given a multi-million pound refurbishment.[^s1]

65157.sum: Wilford Suspension Bridge, also known as Meadows Suspension Bridge, It is a combined suspension footbridge for pedestrians and cyclists, and aqueduct which crosses the River Trent, linking the town of West Bridgford to the Meadows, in the city of Nottingham, England. It also carries a gas main. The bridge is owned by Severn Trent Water.

stories.text: The inn was made from two houses and an outbuilding of the late 17th century, and is listed Grade II. Wilford stayed a village until the later 19th century.[^s1][^s2] With woods around it and riverside amenities such as the Ferry Inn, it attracted many visitors from Nottingham.[^s1] The Notts County goalkeeper Albert Iremonger was its landlord until his death in 1958.[^s1]

stories.text: Around 1361 Gervase de Wilford is thought to have founded a church here, and the building dates from the late 14th century; it was restored in 1890–92 by Naylor and Sale.[^s1][^s2] Inside are two memorials to the poet Henry Kirke White, who drew much inspiration from Wilford and Clifton.[^s1]

stories.text: The Wilford Village and Wilford Lane stops, on line 2 from the city centre to Clifton, opened in August 2015.

Coal was found on the Clifton estate, and work on Clifton Colliery began in 1868. Sir Robert Juckes Clifton, the last of the Clifton baronets, died of typhoid in 1869; the colliery and this toll bridge, both his projects, opened in 1870.

For some 400 years a ferry crossed the Trent here, until a temporary wooden footbridge replaced it in 1864. On 16 June 1870 the toll bridge opened, and pedestrians paid a halfpenny to cross; it is still known locally as the Halfpenny Bridge. It was closed to traffic in 1974, and in 1980 its centre span was replaced by a narrower footbridge. In 2014–15 it was widened again to carry the trams of Nottingham Express Transit, and it is now a tram, pedestrian and cycle bridge.

69731.sum: Wilford Toll Bridge, locally referred to as the 'Halfpenny Bridge', is a tram, pedestrian and cycle bridge in Nottingham, England. It crosses the River Trent between the Meadows and Wilford. It originally opened as a toll bridge for general traffic in 1870, but was closed when declared unsafe in 1974.
